applicability: One single percentage discount of d% taken off one positive ticket price P, where the SALE price S = P·(1 − d/100) is the number you know and P is the number you want. Stated precisely: for every real P > 0 and every d with 0 ≤ d < 100, P = S ÷ (1 − d/100). The divisor 1 − d/100 is the fraction of the price you still pay — call it the keeper — so the rule in words is 'divide the sale price by what you keep', and in the worked example the keeper is 100 − 80 = 20% = 0.2, which makes ÷ 0.2 the same as × 5. This is an exact identity, not an approximation: it is P·k ÷ k = P with k = 1 − d/100, and it is verified here both symbolically for all real P and d < 100 and exhaustively in exact rational arithmetic over the finite domain the draw came from (P = 10t for t in [3,40], d = 10k for k in [1,9]) plus the wider grid d in 0..99, P in 1..500. The condition d < 100 is load-bearing and is exactly what carry_case shows. The rule is stated as division on purpose: the near-universal wrong move is to add the same percentage back onto the sale price, and that is wrong for EVERY d strictly between 0 and 100, because S·(1 + d/100) = P·(1 − d/100)(1 + d/100) = P·(1 − (d/100)²), which is always short of P — by 68 × 1.8 = £122.40 against a true £340 in this example. That failure is also checked exhaustively rather than asserted.
carry_case: d = 100 — a 100%-off item, i.e. a giveaway. The keeper is 100 − 100 = 0, so the rule's own instruction, 'divide by what you keep', asks for a division by zero and returns nothing: the sale price is £0 and £0 ÷ 0 is undefined. This is not a technicality that better arithmetic could rescue. At d = 100 the map P → S collapses every price to the same sale price, so a £340 coat and a £5 mug both ring up as £0 and no method whatever can tell them apart — the information is gone, not merely hard to recover. That makes 100% the exact upper edge of the applicability range: the rule is correct for every d in [0, 100) and undefined at d = 100. The second, far more common failure is not an input but a wrong move — adding the discount back on. Add 80% to the £68 sale price and you get 68 × 1.8 = £122.40, not £340, because the 80% is being taken on the shrunken price instead of the ticket price. Both are verified: division by zero and the collapse at d = 100, and the fact that S·(1 + d/100) < P for every single d in 1..99.

operand_draw.construction: Two integers were drawn, both with the run's seed 369640847, and the worked example is derived from them by two declared linear maps fixed before either draw was seen: discount d = 10 × k with k drawn from [1, 9], and ticket price P = 10 × t (pounds) with t drawn from [3, 40]. The draw gave k = 8 and t = 34, hence d = 80% and P = £340, and the sale price shown to the viewer is the forced consequence S = P(1 − d/100) = 340 × 0.2 = £68. No filter was applied to either draw (rejection_rate 0 on both), so nothing was screened out and every value in both ranges was reachable. The ranges are declared for a stated presentational reason and provably not a mathematical one: over multiples of ten in both places the sale price P(1 − d/100) = t(10 − k) is always a whole number of pounds, so no card ever has to show pence. The rule itself is exact for every d in [0, 100) and every P > 0 — the check verifies that over d = 0..99 and P = 1..500 in exact rationals, far outside the drawn range — so the restriction to round tens cannot be hiding a case where the technique fails. Per §3.4 the draw stands as dealt: d = 80 is a clearance-sale discount rather than a typical 20%, and it was kept rather than re-rolled, which is also the reason the caveat number 68 × 1.8 = £122.40 is so far from £340. The carry case d = 100 is deliberately constructed and deliberately outside the declared range [10, 90], because a counterexample is by definition the input that breaks the rule; §3.4 governs the worked example's operands, not the counterexample. Result 340 is reported as a bare integer string of pounds and is computed as 68 / 0.2 in exact rational arithmetic and cross-checked against 340 × 0.2 = 68, not by replaying the cards.
operand_draw.correlation_disclosure: Both draws used the same seed with different specs, and mulberry32 is a pure function of the seed, so both consumed the same first uniform u ≈ 0.82. The two operands are therefore perfectly rank-correlated rather than independent: k = 8 and t = 34 both sit at the same point of their range. This is disclosed rather than hidden because it lowers the entropy of the pair — but it does not permit hand-picking, since the seed was fixed by the run and both specs were declared before any value was seen, and the alternative (re-rolling until the pair looked independent) is precisely the behaviour §3.4 exists to prevent. Both records replay through verifyDraw().

candidates.verdict: Nearest neighbour: same area, full tag overlap, and it also uses the keeper 1 − d/100. Judged not a duplicate. That lesson goes FORWARD through two discounts and its content is that keepers multiply rather than percentages adding (0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, not 30% off). This one goes BACKWARD through one discount and its content is that the inverse of × k is ÷ k, not + d%. Different direction, different arithmetic operation, different error being corrected, and a viewer who learned to stack keepers still cannot answer 'the tag says £68, what did it cost?' — that is the whole reach of this lesson. It also never shipped: one failure, so the slug is neither blocking nor closed, and no viewer has seen it either way.

Same area and tags. Not a duplicate: a% of b = b% of a is a commutativity observation used to make one forward percentage easier to compute; it never inverts anything, never involves a discount, and has no keeper. Distinct mechanism. Never shipped.

Shipped, and superficially adjacent because it also works from a complement to 100. Not a duplicate: its complement is a distance in units used to build a product of two integers by a digit rule; here the complement is a multiplicative factor and the payoff is a division. No shared step, no shared trigger.

Clear of the ledger, and a real future lesson: +20% then −20% lands at −4%, not 0. Not used here because it is the same 1 − r² expression this lesson's caveat already exposes; shipping both would show the identity twice, so it stays a consequence a viewer can derive rather than its own post.

Clear of the ledger, but it is this exact method with the sign of the change flipped (÷ 1.2 instead of ÷ 0.8). That is one lesson, not two, so it is folded in as the obvious extension rather than run separately — and deliberately not asserted in applicability, see nulls.

nulls.reason: The lesson claims nothing about undoing a percentage INCREASE (strip 20% VAT by dividing by 1.2). The same 'divide by the multiplier' structure applies with multiplier 1 + d/100, but that case is untested here and the on-card rule literally says 'what you keep', which is meaningless for a price that went up. Asserting it without testing it would be a guess, per §3.3.

Nothing is claimed about two or more discounts applied in sequence. Undoing those needs division by the PRODUCT of the keepers, and dividing by a single combined percentage is wrong (20% then 10% is not 30% off). That is a different lesson and is not asserted here.

The identity is exact only when S is the exact discounted price. A real shop rounds S to the nearest penny, and then S ÷ keeper recovers P only up to that rounding — e.g. a price rounded down by 1p and a keeper of 0.2 lands the answer 5p low. No bound on that error is claimed here because none was computed; the drawn range was chosen so the worked example needs no rounding at all.

Claimed for P > 0 only. P = 0 is degenerate (every discount leaves £0, so nothing is recoverable, exactly as in carry_case) and negative prices have no meaning in the discount framing. Neither is asserted.

d > 100 is not claimed. The keeper would be negative and the algebra would return a negative price; whether any shop framing makes that meaningful was not established, so no condition is stated rather than a wrong one being invented.
